newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bickering precedes Chirac visit to Israel.
newsitem.headline: Bickering precedes Chirac visit to Israel.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac prepared for a state visit to Israel, which was preceded by bickering with the Jewish state, by softening his call for the European Union to co-sponsor Arab-Israeli peace talks.

Chirac, who was given a hero's reception during a two-day visit to Syria, starts the Israeli leg of his seven-day regional tour on Monday after the last-minute resolution of a string of diplomatic disputes.

In Damascus, Chirac declared that the Middle East peace process was ailing and prescribed a European salve. But Israel dismissed his call for the European Union to join Washington as a co-sponsor of Arab-Israeli negotiations.

"I would be very careful before I would add more cooks to the broth," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, now locked in U.S.-mediated talks with the Palestinians on implementing of self-rule accords.
"I don't think at this time in such sensitive negotiations it would be wise to introduce another interlocutor," he said.
Israeli and Palestinian negotiators held informal talks late into Sunday in advance of formal talks slated for Monday in Israel's Red Sea resort of Eilat.
Chirac later eased his stance to allay Israeli concerns but insisted on Europe's right to be engaged in peace moves.
"I did not come here to teach people lessons...Naturally we are not trying to force our way in," he said at a joint news conference with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad.
"I am simply saying that we are available and we have valid reasons to be involved, and that a certain balance of things may justify the presence of Europe and of France."

Assad welcomed the French stance. Describing Chirac as "my very dear friend...and a friend of Syria," he thanked the French leader for accomplishing "a task of very great importance for the peace process in the region."

Syria, which won new credit and debt relief from Paris, failed to win French endorsement for its claims that Israel had committed itself before peace talks broke off earlier this year to withdrawing from the occupied Golan Heights.
In Israel, Chirac may face the most difficult stage of his tour, which will also include Palestinian-ruled areas, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt.
In addition to Israel's opposition to French diplomatic ambitions, Chirac's visit was marred in advance by a tiff over his plans to address Palestinian legislators while shunning Israel's parliament.
French officials belatedly added a visit to the Israeli parliament after Knesset Speaker Dan Tichon of Netanyahu's ruling right-wing Likud party threatened to boycott Chirac.
Chirac sparked an earlier diplomatic row when he said he would send Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to Palestine Liberation Organistion headquarters in Jerusalem at Orient House.
After Israel objected to the visit as a threat to its authority in the city it claims as its eternal capital, Chirac decided that de Charette would not accompany him to Israel.
Instead, France will send a junior health minister to Orient House in a move Israel grudgingly accepted behind the diplomatic fiction that his visit would focus on health, not politics.

While Netanyahu swallowed that compromise, he may find Chirac's main message harder to accept -- that Israel can hope for lasting security only if it exchanges land for peace and allows a Palestinian state.
